This measurement of approximately 2.0 cm [Lb = approximately 2.0 cm] at emergence appears to be highly conserved even across disparate local populations, suggesting a strong genetic canalization of hatchling size in this taxon. The juvenile tortoises begin exogenous feeding on succulent vegetation and fallen fruits within days of eclosion, initiating a slow growth trajectory that characterizes this species. During the first several years of life, the young individuals gradually accumulate body mass while their shells harden and develop the characteristic serrated marginal scutes that give the species its common name. Predation pressure from monitor lizards and birds of prey is intense during this juvenile phase, and survivorship to adulthood is correspondingly low. Captive-rearing programs have documented that individuals maintained under optimal thermal and nutritional conditions can complete the initial growth phase more rapidly than wild conspecifics, though the fundamental life-history constraints imposed by this species' slow metabolic pace remain evident.

As the Serrated tortoise progresses through its sub-adult years, a critical developmental threshold is reached when the carapace attains approximately 9.0 cm [Lp = approximately 9.0 cm] in length, marking the onset of gonadal activation and the transition to reproductive maturity. This developmental landmark, characterized by a carapace length of approximately 9.0 cm [Lp = approximately 9.0 cm], triggers a cascade of hormonal changes and the initiation of gametogenesis. The attainment of this milestone is accompanied by a notable increase in body mass, with individuals reaching a wet weight at puberty of roughly 150 g [Wwp = roughly 150 g] under field conditions. This body mass reflects the accumulation of sufficient somatic tissue and fat reserves to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and subsequent egg production. In comparative terms, the wet weight at puberty (150 g) [Wwp = 150 g] of this species is modest relative to larger testudinids such as the congeneric geometric tortoise, yet it represents a substantial investment for an animal inhabiting an environment characterized by unpredictable rainfall and episodic food availability. The condition-dependent nature of this maturation process means that individuals in resource-poor years may delay puberty considerably.

The ultimate carapace length attained by fully grown Serrated tortoises is approximately 15 cm [Li = approximately 15 cm], a dimension that places this species among the smaller members of the Testudinidae. This ultimate carapace length (15 cm) [Li = 15 cm] is reached only after many years of slow, incremental growth, and once achieved, the animal's somatic expansion effectively ceases, with subsequent energy being channeled almost exclusively into reproductive output. Adult individuals are sexually dimorphic in size, with females often attaining the upper end of the size spectrum to accommodate the space required for egg development within the body cavity. Mark-recapture studies conducted in the Northern Cape Province have confirmed that individuals exceeding 14 cm in carapace length are almost invariably reproductively active adults that participate in the annual breeding season. The modest ultimate carapace length (15 cm) [Li = 15 cm] is an ecological correlate of the species' sclerophyllous shrubland habitat, where small body size facilitates thermoregulatory efficiency and reduces absolute food requirements during the dry season. Paleontological records suggest that this size has remained relatively stable over evolutionary timescales.

Reproductive output in the Serrated tortoise is constrained by the species' small body size and the seasonal unpredictability of its environment, with females typically laying 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch] and producing approximately 1 to 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 clutches annually]. The limited clutch size reflects the energetic bottleneck imposed by the female's modest body volume; each egg represents a substantial fraction of the mother's own body mass. Field surveys have noted that many females do not reproduce annually, instead skipping one or more seasons during extended drought periods, which further depresses the population's potential recruitment rate. This conservative reproductive strategy is typical of long-lived chelonians inhabiting stochastic environments.

The lifespan of the Serrated tortoise is remarkably extended for such a small-bodied reptile, with maximum longevity estimated at approximately 188 years [am = approximately 188 years] when maintained under captive conditions at a consistent temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. In the wild, realized lifespans are undoubtedly shorter due to predation, drought-related mortality, and habitat degradation, but the species' physiological capacity for extreme longevity is evident in its low annual adult mortality and delayed reproductive schedule. The temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] used in captive longevity projections approximates the mean annual temperature across much of the species' distribution and is considered representative of the thermal regime under which normal metabolism occurs. Such extraordinary longevity, coupled with a carapace length at birth of just 2.0 cm [Lb = 2.0 cm], illustrates the profound life-history contrast between neonatal vulnerability and decade-spanning adult persistence that defines this species. Ongoing research into telomere dynamics and oxidative stress markers in this species may help elucidate the physiological mechanisms underlying its exceptional resistance to age-related deterioration.
